items.title: Public Sector Motivation: Bureaucratic dimensions’ relation to public servants’ intrinsic motivation in context of self-determination and age
items.abstract: Public servants’ intrinsic motivation—‘their experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work’—is an important correlate of performance (Wright 2004; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Sansone & Harackiewicz 2000) and well-being (Ryan & Deci 2000). Conversely, a lack of intrinsic motivation inhibits the creativity (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Houtgraaf et al. 2021; Houtgraaf et al. 2023) and productivity (Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013) required to provide the effective, user-centered policies/services that citizens need and demand (Clarke et al. 2007; Van Thiel 2017; Torfing 2016). Furthermore, inadequate motivation diminishes public servants’ experienced wellbeing (Barret-Cheetham et al. 2016; Borst 2018) and is associated with dissatisfaction, boreout, burnout, turnover and part-time work in the public sector (Kim 2018; Borst & Knies 2023; Stazyk et al. 2011). Adequate levels of intrinsic motivation are thus of central importance for both workforce performance, well-being and retention. Meanwhile, both practitioners and academics voice that captivating and retaining public servants is increasingly becoming a challenge—especially with more junior public servants. In general, attracting and retaining an intrinsically motivated workforce appears difficult due to numerous developments in both the nature of work and the nature of employees (Davidesque et al. 2020; Twenge et al. 2010; Cahill et al. 2012). In the public sector too, sustainable employment is of growing concern, illustrated by efforts to understand and safeguard public servants’ well-being, performance and retention (Van der Meer et al. 2022; Borst & Knies 2023; Johari et al. 2019). The challenges of captivating and retaining seems especially true for employees from more recent generations—or at least of younger age (Schröder 2023)—that are argued to have different and more pronounced expectations and preferences relating to work (Waworuntu et al. 2022). In the Netherlands, for example, the translated ‘captivate and bind’ programs sprout throughout the public sector in an alarmed effort to retain (junior) public servants (Binnenlands Bestuur 2024). However, our knowledge regarding intrinsic motivation amidst bureaucratic constraints falls short on two major accounts. Firstly, insight is lacking on whether a lack of intrinsic motivation is an issue in the public sector as a result of bureaucratic constraints and through what mechanisms this would or would not occur. On the one hand, bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization arguably have several negative effects that relate to a lack of intrinsic motivation (Giauque et al. 2012; George et al. 2021; Lavigna 2013; Serhan et al. 2018). On the other hand, such bureaucratic constraints might not lead to amotivation as public servants’ motivation is argued to be a relatively stable concept (Baldwin 1990; Houtgraaf & Ropes in press) and because public servants’ argued idiosyncratic personality may actually lead them to value bureaucratic elements (Leisha & DeHart-Davis 2007; Merton 1940; Bozeman & Rainey 1998). Applying Self-Determination Theory and assessing whether bureaucratic constraints as forms of external locus of control diminish public servants’ sense of autonomy and competence and thereby lead to amotivation (Ryan & Deci 2000, see also Ekval 1996) would provide insight on underlying mechanisms but has not been applied. Secondly, insight is lacking on the role of age/generation, despite evidence pointing towards a significant moderating function. Millennials and more recent generations are argued to assign particular value to elements of autonomy and positive hierarchical feedback relating to competence in their work (Waworuntu et al. 2022), which appears at odds with bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization typically present in the public sector that may stifle such senses of autonomy and competence (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000; Ekval 1996). Moreover, recent findings dispute that such differences relating to work motivation and preferences are a result of generational differences but a function of age (Schröder 2023). In short, insight is lacking on whether and why bureaucratic constraints relate to amotivation, what role age/generation plays and thus what strategies and tactics to employ in order to captivate and retain public servants—especially junior ones. Therefore, the goal of this study was to scrutinize whether and how bureaucratic dimensions relate to public servants’ intrinsic motivation whilst paying particular attention to self-determination as an underlying mechanism and the role of age. To these ends, several analyses are conducted on cross-sectional data from 1158 public servants working in a range of Dutch public sector organizations to answer the research question: ‘Through which mechanisms do levels of public servants’ intrinsic motivation correlate with the presence of bureaucratic dimensions, taking into account age?’. Scrutinizing these mechanisms allowed for detailed insights in mechanisms of intrinsic motivation and how to safeguard it in the public sector context, especially among specific age groups. The ensuing results provide public sector practitioners, managers, HR-departments and training organizations with avenues on whether and how to effectively counter adverse effects of bureaucratic dimensions on public servants’ motivation in order to captivate and retain public servants’ and in turn improve their performance, wellbeing and sustainable employment. MOTIVATION AMIDST BUREAUCRATIC CONSTRAINTS Intrinsic motivation and Self-Determination Theory Intrinsic motivation encompasses an experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work that stems from the employee itself, instead of external factors (Wright 2004; Ryan & Deci 2000; Li et al. 2015). According to Self-Determination Theory, the central characteristic of intrinsic motivation is that it stems from an internal locus of control whereby the individual experiences a control over its own actions and outcomes, instead of an external locus of control whereby the individual experiences that its actions and outcomes are determined by external factors such as managers or rules (Deci & Ryan 1985; Li et al. 2015). In more detail, according to Self-Determination Theory, senses of autonomy, competence and relatedness are essential psychological needs that can be satisfied or frustrated and thus determine the degree of an internal locus of control and experience of intrinsic motivation: the individual has to perceive itself as an autonomous actor that is able and capable of acting in correspondence with its values and goals (Chen et al. 2015; Deci & Ryan 1985). External locus of control, however, may lead to a lack of perceived internal locus of control, hampering intrinsic motivation (Bénabou & Tirole 2003; Deci and Ryan 1985) and leading to amotivation whereby the enjoyment, interest and satisfaction of work becomes increasingly absent (Howard et al., 2016). In general, intrinsic motivation is perceived as beneficial for performance and well-being (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Ryan & Deci 2000; Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013), which results in the reasoning that an impairing external locus of control that may hamper employees’ intrinsic motivation ought to be avoided. When assessing intrinsic motivation, it is important to determine whether the concept is approached as an attitude or a state, depending on the goal and timeline of assessment. If considered an attitude, intrinsic motivation is assessed based on an individual’s recall over a longer period of time based on the remembering-self, thereby leading to a more average and stable assessment of the level of intrinsic motivation, whereas if considered a state, intrinsic motivation is assessed on based on an individual’s experience in the current moment based on the experiencing-self, thereby leading to accurate but momentarily and fluctuating assessments of levels of intrinsic motivation (Kahneman & Riis 2005). As the goal of this study concerns assessing how individuals recall their work contexts and attitudes in general and on average in order to assess relations, intrinsic motivation is approached and measured as an attitude in this study (Lee & Choi 2003). Formalization as external locus of control Formalization—the degree to which work related processes and interactions are generally governed by formal rules, standard policies and procedures (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000)—can be perceived as representing external locus of control that may hamper public servants’ intrinsic motivation. Formalization is a typical bureaucratic dimension of mechanistic organizations (Brown 2014) and although public sector reforms have aimed at reduction of formalization (Van Thiel 2001), public sector organizations are characterized as featuring at least certain levels of formalization (Borins 2010; Boyne 2002; Boye et al. 2022; Houtgraaf et al. 2023). The object of such bureaucratic principles as expressed in formalization is to achieve stability, standardization and to avoid flexibility and change (Ekval 1996) by controlling employee behavior (Hirst et al. 2009). As such, formalization is a clear example of external locus of control that may hamper intrinsic motivation. Arguably, the underlying mechanisms are twofold. On the one hand, the rules and procedures imposed by formalization may frustrate a sense of autonomy as the individual might not be able to act as it would without these external controls (Hirst et al. 2009). On the other hand, formalization its rules and procedures are related to passive, rule-bound and anxious behavior to stay inside established boundaries (Ekval 1996), which may frustrate a sense of competence as the individual might feel less capable and efficacious in conducting work as a result of the external controls (Au 2015). items.title: Purely robotic ileocystoplasty in children: why not? First case in Spain
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: We present the first case of pediatric ileocystoplasty using a purely robotic approach in Spain. CASE REPORT: 12-year-old male with neurogenic bladder of low capacity and high pressures. After failure of conservative treatment, bladder augmentation with ileum patch was decided upon. Surgery was carried out using a purely robotic approach with 4 robotic and 2 accessory ports. Surgery duration was 380 minutes in total, without intraoperative complications. He was discharged 2 weeks after cystographic control. During 32-months follow-up, he has remained continent. DISCUSSION: The minimal invasion, surgical precision and ergonomics made the robotic approach an optimal option for complex surgical techniques. Given the little availability of the robot and the low pediatric volume, its standardization is a challenge. Our accumulated experience is consistent with the current literature and shows promising surgical and esthetic results. We hope this case report will contribute to the divulgation and progressive introduction of robotic surgery in our daily lives.

items.title: Purpose and Nonprofit Enterprise
items.abstract: Nonprofit enterprise is responsible for a large share of economic activity across the globe. And yet, leading theories fail to explain why nonprofit business survives and even thrives across a vast number of industries, ranging from artificial intelligence to beer brewing, despite an absence of shareholder control. Indeed, as shareholder ownership and intervention rights have become the core component of successful corporate governance, this success is all the more surprising.We offer a novel “purposeful enterprise” theory to explain the puzzling success of nonprofit enterprises. Drawing on research in behavioral economics and organizational science, we argue that organizational purpose can serve as a substitute for shareholder control and monitoring, by mitigating managerial agency costs and aligning employee incentives. Nonprofit enterprise may also promote value creation by improving the stability of the entity. Our theory clarifies why nonprofit businesses and other related purposeful enterprises have thrived in certain industries and not others. It also sheds light on fundamental debates in corporate law, including that of the corporation’s purpose in society. In particular, it suggests that shareholder ownership and control is not the only means of addressing agency costs and improving organizational efficiency.

items.title: Qualitative interview study of strategies to support healthcare personnel mental health through an occupational health lens
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Employee Occupational Health ('occupational health') clinicians have expansive perspectives of the experience of healthcare personnel. Integrating mental health into the purview of occupational health is a newer approach that could combat historical limitations of healthcare personnel mental health programmes, which have been isolated and underused. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to document innovation and opportunities for supporting healthcare personnel mental health through occupational health clinicians. This work was part of a national qualitative needs assessment of employee occupational health clinicians during COVID-19 who were very much at the centre of organisational responses. DESIGN: This qualitative needs assessment included key informant interviews obtained using snowball sampling methods. PARTICIPANTS: We interviewed 43 US Veterans Health Administration occupational health clinicians from 29 facilities. APPROACH: This analysis focused on personnel mental health needs and opportunities, using consensus coding of interview transcripts and modified member checking. KEY RESULTS: Three major opportunities to support mental health through occupational health involved: (1) expanded mental health needs of healthcare personnel, including opportunities to support work-related concerns (eg, traumatic deployments), home-based concerns and bereavement (eg, working with chaplains); (2) leveraging expanded roles and protocols to address healthcare personnel mental health concerns, including opportunities in expanding occupational health roles, cross-disciplinary partnerships (eg, with employee assistance programmes (EAP)) and process/protocol (eg, acute suicidal ideation pathways) and (3) need for supporting occupational health clinicians' own mental health, including opportunities to address overwork/burn-out with adequate staffing/resources. CONCLUSIONS: Occupational health can enact strategies to support personnel mental health: to structurally sustain attention, use social cognition tools (eg, suicidality protocols or expanded job descriptions); to leverage distributed attention, enhance interdisciplinary collaboration (eg, chaplains for bereavement support or EAP) and to equip systems with resources and allow for flexibility during crises, including increased staffing.

items.title: Quantitative analysis of landscape changes in geoparks combined with GIS
items.abstract: Geoparks are both the concentration of valuable geological remains and an important carrier of tourism activities. Relying on a geographic information system (GIS), this project takes the landscape change of a geopark from 2005 to 2020 as an example, and after processing the remote sensing images, quantitative analysis is carried out by using the landscape pattern index method, which reveals the landscape change characteristics of the sample geopark. The data related to natural and human factors was collected, and the driving factors of landscape changes in geoparks were analyzed by combining probes. The main landscape types of the sample geoparks are cropland, woodland, and rocky desertification land, and the study period presents landscape changes of decreasing cropland area (22.96%), fluctuating woodland area, and increasing desertification area (37.40%), and the development of the park landscape changes presents irregularity and complexity. The main drivers of landscape change in geoparks are geological conditions, topography and geomorphology, vegetation, economic development capacity, and ecological environment quality (q value = 0.438~0.521), of which economic development capacity and ecological environment quality play a dominant role in the interaction of factors (0.86).

items.abstract: Purpose: The aim of this article is to identify effective measures to prevent silent departures declared by managers.The following research problems were formulated: what are the causes of the phenomenon of silent departures as perceived by managers?What actions do managers believe are most effective in counteracting silent departures in the organisations they manage?Design/methodology/approach: The research problems were addressed using a narrative literature review method and a qualitative research study (FGI) conducted with a sample of 10 managers representing the corporate sector.Findings: The causes of quiet quitting can be psychological, social, economic or managerial.Among the most important psychological causes of quiet quitting are: changes in the individual value system consisting in the lowering of the rank of career as a determinant of success in life, an increase in the intensity of individualistic and narcissistic attitudes, an increase in the intensity of hedonistic needs going hand in hand with a decrease in psychological resilience, a sense of disillusionment with relationships in the work environment.Among the social causes, changes in the social system of values were identified, consisting in an increase in the importance of individualism and a decrease in the ethos of work in favour of individual wellbeing.Among
